one_line_idea: Log-depth versus metric-depth regression targets act as fixed per-pixel gradient preconditioners, so the log target should win exactly on scenes whose depth-range ratio exceeds a predictable threshold and be irrelevant on shallow-range scenes.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Monocular depth pipelines variously regress metric depth, log depth, or inverse depth, and the choice is usually inherited from prior codebases rather than derived; papers rarely state when the choice matters.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The target parameterization acts as a diagonal preconditioner on per-pixel gradients: metric-depth L1 gives far pixels gradient magnitudes proportional to their absolute error scale, so on wide-range scenes far regions dominate the update budget and near-field structure is starved; log-depth equalizes relative-error gradients across the range. The active ingredient is gradient allocation, not representational capacity.

Kill the idea if the advantage is flat across range bins (spread < 3% relative) or if near-field error under metric-depth training does not show the predicted gradient starvation signature (near-field per-pixel gradient share < 0.5x that of log training).
why_important: If target choice is a preconditioner, the community can predict the right parameterization per dataset from a one-pass depth-histogram statistic instead of folklore, and the same logic transfers to any dense regression target with heavy-tailed scale.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Log and inverse depth targets are standard practice, but a pre-registered scene-conditional crossover law tied to measured per-pixel gradient shares appears untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train matched networks on NYU Depth v2 and KITTI with metric, log, and inverse targets; log per-pixel gradient magnitude by depth decile during training; evaluate AbsRel stratified by scene depth-range ratio.
main_risk: Loss clamping and dataset-specific depth caps may already mimic log-like gradient allocation, shrinking the measurable gap.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Log/inverse depth is treated as a blanket best practice justified by perceptual scale, with no scene-conditional prediction attached.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The benefit may come from target-distribution normalization (variance matching to init scale) rather than per-pixel gradient allocation, in which case a global affine rescaling of metric depth would suffice and the range-ratio law would fail.

core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Early in training, a nontrivial fraction of pixels sit at large angular error where the angular loss Jacobian is ill-conditioned; these pixels emit gradient spikes that destabilize shared features, and the damage is done in the first fraction of training when spike frequency is highest.

why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Loss switching is used ad hoc; tying the switch point to measured gradient-spike statistics of manifold-valued targets appears unexplored.

why_important: It turns an arbitrary head-design choice into a predictable dynamics knob, with direct consequences for open-vocabulary and partially labeled settings where sigmoids are mandatory and the coupling loss must be replaced by something else.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Softmax-vs-sigmoid comparisons exist for final accuracy; the within-run anti-correlation signature and boundary-band confusion decomposition appear unexamined.

one_line_idea: Dice loss is an implicit instance-size reweighting schedule whose strength grows as predictions sharpen, predicting that dice beats cross-entropy only when the target size distribution is heavy-tailed beyond a measurable threshold.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Dice and cross-entropy dominate segmentation training and their relative merits are folklore (dice for imbalance, CE for stability), but no quantitative rule tells a practitioner which to use on a given dataset.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Dice normalizes each structure's contribution by its predicted+true size, so per-pixel gradients scale inversely with structure size, and this reweighting intensifies during training as soft predictions contract toward the structure; dice-vs-CE outcomes are therefore governed by the tail exponent of the size distribution, not by class imbalance per se.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Across datasets and resampled variants engineered to vary the structure-size tail (subsampling large instances), the dice-minus-CE gap will flip sign at a consistent tail statistic (within a factor of 2 across datasets), and time-resolved per-size gradient shares will show dice's small-structure share growing by at least 2x over training. Kill the idea if the sign flip point varies by more than 10x across datasets or if dice's gradient share is time-constant (within 20%).
why_important: It replaces the imbalance folklore with a testable size-tail law and a one-pass dataset statistic that predicts loss choice, and reveals that the loss embeds a hidden curriculum whose strength practitioners never scheduled deliberately.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Dice gradient analyses exist for medical imbalance; the time-intensifying reweighting dynamics and cross-dataset sign-flip law appear untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train U-Net/DeepLabv3+ on Cityscapes instances and a resampled-size-tail variant with dice vs CE; log per-size-decile gradient shares over training; locate the gap sign flip as a function of tail statistic.
main_risk: Dice's batch-level formulation differs across codebases (per-image vs per-batch normalization), which changes the reweighting math and must be fixed and reported.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Dice is preferred whenever foreground is rare, a class-imbalance story that ignores size-distribution shape and training-time dynamics.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The gap may be dominated by dice's different treatment of empty predictions (denominator instability), a numerical artifact independent of size tails.
fastest_falsification_experiment: DeepLabv3+ ResNet-50 (mmsegmentation, public) on Cityscapes (public) plus two size-resampled variants, 2 losses x 3 datasets x 2 seeds at 20k iterations: about 2.5 days on one A100.

one_line_idea: Structured surrogate losses like Lovász hinge help exactly when a model's errors are spatially clustered, because their pixel-gradient coupling coordinates updates within an error blob, predicting the gain from a pre-training error-autocorrelation measurement.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Lovász-softmax and similar IoU surrogates beat cross-entropy in some segmentation setups and not others, and the community has no account of which setups benefit.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] These losses couple gradients across pixels of the same class within an image (through the sorted-error construction), effectively making coordinated blob-level corrections; when errors are spatially independent the coupling adds variance without benefit, so the spatial autocorrelation length of the error field determines the sign of the effect.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Across 8 model-dataset configurations, the Lovász-minus-CE mIoU gap will correlate with pre-measured error autocorrelation length at Spearman rho >= 0.6, and configurations with autocorrelation below 4 pixels will show gaps within +-0.3 mIoU. Kill the idea if rho < 0.25 or if spatially-shuffled-error controls (patch-permuted training images) preserve the Lovász advantage, which would locate the mechanism elsewhere.
why_important: It converts an unreliable loss-choice folklore into a cheap pre-measurement rule and identifies gradient coupling, not metric alignment, as the operative property of structured surrogates.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Lovász losses are motivated as IoU surrogates (metric alignment); the error-autocorrelation moderator and the coupling mechanism appear untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Take 8 public segmentation configs spanning CNN/transformer and two datasets; measure baseline error autocorrelation; retrain each with Lovász; correlate gap with autocorrelation; add one patch-permuted control.
main_risk: Error autocorrelation and dataset identity are confounded; the resampled and permuted controls are essential to break the confound, adding arms.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Structured surrogates are believed to help because they optimize the evaluation metric more directly, implying dataset-independent gains.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The sorted-error construction also changes the effective example weighting (hardest pixels dominate), which is an OHEM-like mechanism that could explain gains without any spatial-coupling story.
fastest_falsification_experiment: SegFormer-B0 and DeepLabv3+ (both public) on Cityscapes and ADE20K (public), 8 configs x 2 losses at short 20k schedules: about 4 days on one A100; autocorrelation measurement is post-hoc on saved logits.

one_line_idea: Focal loss is functionally an annealed hard-pixel selection schedule: replacing it with explicit top-k pixel selection whose k follows focal's shrinking effective-support trajectory should reproduce its gains, killing the reweighting-form story.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Focal loss is the default for dense detection and many segmentation setups, credited to its specific polynomial down-weighting form; countless variants tweak the form.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] What matters is not the weighting form but the induced trajectory of effective support: as the model improves, the fraction of pixels with non-negligible focal gradient shrinks, making focal an automatic anneal from all-pixel to hard-pixel training; any selection scheme matching that support trajectory will match focal.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Explicit top-k cross-entropy with k(t) matched to focal's measured effective-support trajectory will come within 0.3 AP of focal on COCO with RetinaNet, while fixed-k arms will lose at least 1.0 AP, establishing the trajectory (not the form) as the active ingredient. Kill the idea if trajectory-matched top-k lags focal by more than 1.0 AP, which would mean the soft weighting form carries independent value.
why_important: A positive result collapses the focal-variant cottage industry into a single scheduling principle and gives a knob (support trajectory) that can be designed directly instead of through loss-form tinkering.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Focal-vs-OHEM comparisons exist at fixed settings; matching the measured support trajectory as the equivalence variable appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train RetinaNet-R50 on COCO with focal; log the effective-support trajectory (fraction of pixels contributing 90% of gradient); retrain with top-k CE using that trajectory and with fixed k; compare AP over 2 seeds.
main_risk: Focal's soft weighting also affects the gradient magnitude distribution within the selected set; a hybrid arm (soft weighting inside matched support) may be needed to fully attribute the effect.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] The focal form itself (the gamma exponent) is treated as the innovation, as evidenced by the many form-variant papers.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Hard selection introduces gradient discontinuities at the k-th boundary that soft weighting avoids, which could destabilize training in ways trajectory matching cannot fix.
fastest_falsification_experiment: RetinaNet-R50 (mmdetection, public) on COCO (public) at 1x schedule, 4 arms x 2 seeds: about 3 days on one A100; support-trajectory logging is a cheap training hook.

one_line_idea: Cross-entropy training drives dense-head logit norms to grow roughly logarithmically, imposing a hidden effective-LR decay on decision geometry; norm-controlled heads should therefore need explicit schedule compensation, exposing an unacknowledged coupling between loss and schedule.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Unregularized CE training inflates logit magnitudes over time in classification; dense prediction inherits this, but schedules are designed as if the loss surface were time-stationary.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Growing logit norms shrink softmax gradients for correctly classified pixels, acting as an implicit per-pixel LR decay concentrated on easy regions; part of what cosine decay 'does' for segmentation is redundant with this implicit decay, so fixing the logit norm (weight-normalized head with fixed temperature) redistributes when and where learning happens and requires a different explicit schedule to match.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] With head logit norms fixed, the best constant-LR run will end at least 1.0 mIoU below the norm-free baseline under the baseline's schedule, but re-tuning only the decay endpoint will close the gap to within 0.3 mIoU, with easy-region (interior) accuracy acquisition measurably delayed (>= 15% more steps to 95% of final interior accuracy). Kill the idea if fixed-norm training matches the baseline under the identical schedule within 0.2 mIoU, which would mean implicit logit-norm decay plays no scheduling role in dense prediction.
why_important: Schedules and losses are tuned as independent modules everywhere; demonstrating a quantitative interaction forces joint reporting and explains cross-paper schedule irreproducibility when head parameterizations differ.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Logit-norm growth is studied for classification margins; its role as an implicit spatially-selective schedule in dense prediction appears unexamined.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train SegFormer-B0 on ADE20K with standard head vs weight-normalized fixed-temperature head under identical schedules, then re-tune the schedule for the fixed-norm arm; track interior-vs-boundary acquisition curves and logit-norm trajectories.
main_risk: Weight decay already partially controls logit norms, so the norm-free baseline must log actual norm growth to confirm the manipulated variable moved.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] LR schedules are treated as loss-independent, and logit growth as a margin/regularization topic irrelevant to scheduling.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Dense heads share features across pixels, so per-pixel implicit decay may wash out at the shared-feature level where the schedule actually operates.
fastest_falsification_experiment: SegFormer-B0 (public) on ADE20K (public), 3 arms x 2 seeds at 40k iterations: about 2.5 days on one A100; logit-norm logging is free.

one_line_idea: Boundary-region learning is gradient-starved until interiors saturate, making interior-then-boundary acquisition an optimization-forced order; boundary emphasis should therefore only matter under short training budgets, with a predictable crossover.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Numerous papers report gains from emphasizing boundary regions in segmentation losses, while others find no benefit, and long-schedule reproductions often shrink the gains; the field lacks a governing account.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Early in training, interior pixels dominate the gradient budget because they are numerous and initially wrong; boundary pixels receive meaningful gradient only after interiors saturate. Boundary emphasis merely pulls this phase forward, so its value decays with budget and vanishes when the natural boundary phase completes within the schedule.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] At a 25% budget, boundary-band reweighting will improve boundary F-score by at least 2 points; at full budget the improvement will fall below 0.5 points, and time-resolved gradient shares will show the natural boundary-phase onset scaling with interior saturation time (correlation r >= 0.7 across 6 configs). Kill the idea if boundary emphasis keeps helping by >= 1.5 points at 2x the standard budget, which would falsify the phase-completion account in favor of a permanent optimization barrier at boundaries.
why_important: It explains contradictory boundary-loss literature with a single budget-dependent law, tells practitioners when boundary emphasis is worth it, and reframes acquisition order as gradient-budget allocation that schedules can manipulate.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Boundary losses are abundant; the budget-crossover law and the interior-saturation timing prediction appear untested. This idea deliberately makes no claim about labeling practices; it is purely an optimization-dynamics account.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train DeepLabv3+ on Cityscapes at 25/50/100/200% budgets with and without boundary-band reweighting; log per-band gradient shares; measure boundary F-score and trimap accuracy at each budget.
main_risk: Boundary metrics are sensitive to the band width definition; pre-registering band widths (4 and 8 px) avoids post-hoc metric shopping.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Boundary emphasis is viewed as adding information the plain loss lacks, implying budget-independent gains.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Boundary pixels may be starved by irreducible ambiguity rather than gradient competition, in which case no budget extension completes the phase and the 2x-budget arm will keep showing gains.
fastest_falsification_experiment: DeepLabv3+ R50 (mmsegmentation, public) on Cityscapes (public), 4 budgets x 2 arms x 2 seeds: about 3.5 days on one A100 (short budgets dominate the grid cheaply).

one_line_idea: Class-frequency loss reweighting interacts destructively with momentum: rare-class gradient bursts get smeared into subsequent unrelated batches, so reweighting gains should shrink as momentum grows, an interaction nobody tunes for.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Inverse-frequency loss weighting is a default remedy for class imbalance in segmentation, and momentum 0.9 is a default optimizer setting; they are tuned independently in every codebase.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Rare classes appear in occasional bursts; amplifying their loss creates large transient gradients that momentum carries into many following steps where the rare class is absent, applying stale rare-class updates against unrelated batches and partially undoing the intended effect; lower momentum or momentum-reset-on-burst should restore the reweighting benefit.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] The rare-class IoU benefit of 10x reweighting will be at least 2x larger at momentum 0.5 than at momentum 0.99 on Cityscapes rare classes, and per-step interference (cosine between the momentum buffer and current batch gradient after rare bursts) will be significantly more negative under high momentum (mean cosine <= -0.05 vs >= -0.01). Kill the idea if the reweighting benefit is momentum-independent within 20% or if the interference cosine shows no burst-conditioned structure.
why_important: This is distinct from the occupied finding W13-P1-D-031 (reweighting as disguised score recalibration): here the claim is a mechanistic optimizer interaction that predicts WHEN reweighting works at all, with a cheap fix (burst-conditioned momentum handling) if confirmed.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Loss reweighting and momentum are both ancient, but their interaction through burst timing appears unmeasured in dense prediction.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Grid over momentum {0.5, 0.9, 0.99} x reweighting {1x, 10x} on Cityscapes with DeepLabv3+, log momentum-buffer/batch-gradient cosines around rare-class bursts, compare rare-class IoU deltas.
main_risk: Adam's per-parameter normalization complicates the story relative to SGD+momentum; running SGD first isolates the mechanism, with an Adam arm as generalization check.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Reweighting strength and momentum are treated as orthogonal hyperparameters with no interaction worth reporting.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Momentum smearing may actually help rare classes by extending their effective presence across steps (a mild replay), making the interaction positive rather than destructive.
fastest_falsification_experiment: DeepLabv3+ R50 (public) on Cityscapes (public), 6 arms x 2 seeds at 20k iterations with SGD: about 2 days on one A100.

one_line_idea: Whether combining two dense losses helps is determined by the spatial structure of their per-pixel gradient disagreement: structured disagreement (different losses own different pixel populations) yields complementary gains, diffuse disagreement yields averaging.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Compound losses (e.g., CE+dice) are ubiquitous defaults in dense prediction, yet combination outcomes vary by task and no principle distinguishes complementary pairs from redundant or conflicting ones.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Two losses help jointly when their per-pixel gradient sign disagreements concentrate on distinct, coherent pixel populations (e.g., one loss dominates boundaries, the other interiors), so each population gets a consistent signal; when disagreement is spatially diffuse the combination merely averages and adds variance.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Across 10 loss pairs on two segmentation datasets, a disagreement-structure index (mutual information between disagreement indicator and pixel-population labels) will separate pairs whose combination beats both singles from pairs that do not, with AUC >= 0.8. Kill the idea if AUC < 0.6, or if a pair with near-zero structured disagreement still shows >= 1.0 mIoU combination synergy, indicating a mechanism beyond gradient-population structure.
why_important: A validated structure test would let practitioners screen loss combinations with a half-epoch measurement instead of full factorial training, and would explain why the same compound loss helps on one dataset and not another.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Gradient-conflict analyses exist for multi-task learning across tasks; applying population-structured conflict analysis to same-task loss combination appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: For 10 documented loss pairs, measure disagreement structure on a half-epoch probe run, then train all singles and combinations to convergence and test whether the index predicts synergy sign.
main_risk: Defining pixel populations (boundary bands, size classes, frequency bands) involves choices; pre-registering three population partitions and requiring consistency guards against index shopping.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Compound losses are assumed beneficial by default (belt and suspenders), with failures attributed to weighting rather than structural redundancy.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Synergy might be driven by optimization-trajectory effects (early-phase stabilization) that a static disagreement snapshot cannot capture, requiring trajectory-resolved measurement.

one_line_idea: Temperature in pixel-level contrastive objectives sets the effective number of negatives that receive gradient, and the right temperature is determined by the intra-class visual diversity of the dataset, predicting opposite tuning directions for homogeneous versus diverse datasets.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Dense/pixel contrastive pretraining uses a temperature copied from image-level recipes (around 0.07-0.2), and tuning guidance is folklore; dense settings differ because negatives include many same-image, same-class pixels.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Low temperature concentrates gradient on the hardest negatives; in dense settings the hardest negatives for diverse classes are frequently semantically same-class pixels (other instances, distant parts), so low temperature actively teaches wrong invariances on diverse datasets while sharpening useful boundaries on homogeneous ones; the optimal temperature therefore increases with measured intra-class feature diversity.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Across dataset variants with engineered intra-class diversity (subsetting classes by appearance spread), optimal temperature (by downstream linear-probe mIoU) will shift monotonically with the diversity statistic, moving by at least 2x between extremes, and hardest-negative composition will show >= 30% same-class contamination at low temperature on diverse data. Kill the idea if optimal temperature moves by under 30% across the diversity range or if same-class contamination is uncorrelated with the diversity statistic.
why_important: It gives dense contrastive pretraining a principled temperature rule based on a measurable dataset statistic and identifies a failure mode (hard-negative same-class contamination) specific to dense objectives, distinct from the boundary-assignment pathology already occupied by W13-P1-E-075.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Temperature analyses exist for image-level contrastive learning; the dense-specific same-class contamination account with a diversity-conditioned tuning law appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Pretrain pixel-contrastive ResNet-50 on Cityscapes-derived variants with three diversity levels x four temperatures; measure hardest-negative composition during training and linear-probe segmentation after.
main_risk: Diversity manipulation by class subsetting also changes class count and data volume; matched-size controls are required.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Temperature is treated as a universal constant of contrastive learning, transferred unchanged from image-level recipes to dense variants.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Projection-head geometry may absorb temperature differences, making downstream probes insensitive to the manipulated variable even if contamination changes.
fastest_falsification_experiment: ResNet-50 (torchvision init, public) pixel-contrastive pretraining on Cityscapes (public) at 12 arms x 50 epochs reduced scale: about 4 days on one A100; probes are cheap.

one_line_idea: Pairwise/structured consistency terms in dense losses act mostly as spatial gradient-noise dampers, so replacing them with content-blind local gradient smoothing should reproduce the bulk of their reported gains.

core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The operative effect of these terms is variance reduction: they average gradient signals over neighborhoods, damping per-pixel supervision noise; the structural content (affinity correctness) is mostly irrelevant, so content-blind smoothing of the per-pixel gradient field with a matched kernel should recover most of the benefit.

one_line_idea: Asymmetric region losses (Tversky-style) change ranking quality only when class overlap in feature space is itself asymmetric; otherwise they merely slide along the precision-recall curve, which threshold-free ranking metrics will expose.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Tversky-style asymmetric losses are tuned to trade false positives against false negatives in segmentation, and papers report improvements on thresholded metrics after tuning the asymmetry.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] If the learned score function's ranking of pixels is unchanged, asymmetry only moves the operating point, which post-hoc threshold selection achieves for free; asymmetry genuinely improves ranking only when the two error types originate from feature-space regions of different learnability, an asymmetry measurable before training.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Across 6 public binary-segmentation setups, pixel-ranking quality (area under the pixel precision-recall curve) will differ between symmetric and best-asymmetric training by under 1% in setups with symmetric feature overlap, while setups with measured asymmetric overlap (one error type concentrated in low-density feature regions) will show >= 3% AUPRC gains. Kill the idea if ranking gains appear without measured overlap asymmetry in 2+ setups, or if no setup with asymmetry shows gains.
why_important: It separates a real training-dynamics effect from operating-point relabeling, protecting the literature from a systematic evaluation confound while specifying exactly when asymmetric objectives are worth training (not just thresholding).
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Tversky-style tuning is widespread; adjudicating via threshold-free ranking metrics plus a pre-measured overlap-asymmetry statistic appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train symmetric vs swept-asymmetry losses on 6 binary segmentation tasks; evaluate pixel AUPRC (threshold-free) alongside thresholded metrics; measure feature-overlap asymmetry from a probe model's score distributions per error type.
main_risk: AUPRC on highly imbalanced pixels is noisy; bootstrap confidence intervals and fixed evaluation pixel samples are needed.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Asymmetric losses are believed to teach the model different decision behavior, with thresholded-metric gains taken as evidence of better learning.

core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The mean criterion is dominated by frequent classes that peak (and start overfitting) early, so the selected checkpoint predates rare-class convergence by a margin that grows with acquisition stagger; selecting per-class-optimal checkpoints (or stopping on a stagger-aware criterion) recovers rare-class accuracy at negligible frequent-class cost because their overfitting slope is shallow.

why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Staggered class learning is folk-observed; quantifying the stopping-rule tax and the recovery from stagger-aware selection appears new.

why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Pixel-sampled losses exist ad hoc; the correlation-length law with architecture-dependent knee prediction appears new.

problem: [KNOWN FACT] After loss spikes, training curves visibly recover and practitioners treat the incident as closed once aggregate loss returns to trend; whether recovery is uniform across the structured output is unexamined.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Spikes disproportionately corrupt low-redundancy knowledge (rare-class prototypes, fine boundary placements) whose gradient signal is too sparse to rebuild quickly, while high-redundancy knowledge (frequent-class interiors) re-converges almost immediately; therefore post-spike deficits persist selectively, spike-heavy runs end measurably worse on rare/boundary metrics at matched final aggregate loss, and a short post-spike replay of rare-class-dense content erases the selective deficit.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Injecting controlled spikes (temporary 10x LR for 20 steps) at three points in Cityscapes training, frequent-class interior accuracy will recover to control-trajectory levels within 500 steps while the rarest-quintile class IoU remains at least 1.0 below control for 5000+ steps, spike-injected runs will end at least 0.8 IoU behind controls on rare classes despite matching mean loss within 1%, and targeted replay after spikes will close at least 60% of the persistent gap. Kill the idea if recovery timescales differ by less than 2x across populations or final rare-class deficits are under 0.3 IoU.
why_important: It shows that stability incidents leave class-selective scars invisible to the curves everyone monitors, justifying spike-history reporting and targeted-replay remediation, and quantifies knowledge redundancy as the variable governing what training forgets under perturbation.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Spike recovery is assessed on aggregate losses in practice; population-resolved hysteresis measurement with a remediation arm appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Controlled spike injection at pre-registered points vs twin controls; population-resolved accuracy tracking at high checkpoint frequency; targeted-replay remediation arms over 3 seeds.
main_risk: Injected spikes must approximate natural ones; a small observational validation on naturally spiking runs (from the trigger-mining study design) checks the injection's ecological validity.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] A recovered loss curve means a recovered model; spike incidents are not tracked as run metadata anywhere.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Optimizer state (Adam second moments) may buffer rare-class parameters against spikes precisely because their gradients are sparse, inverting the predicted vulnerability ordering.
fastest_falsification_experiment: DeepLabv3+ R50 (public) on Cityscapes (public), 3 injection points x {spike, control, spike+replay} x 3 seeds at 40k iterations: about 3.5 days on one A100.

one_line_idea: Tail-averaging (SWA-style) of dense-training checkpoints improves interiors but degrades or fails to improve boundary placement when averaged checkpoints still disagree structurally at boundaries, making the disagreement decomposition, not flat-minima intuition, the correct adoption criterion.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Stochastic weight averaging over late-training checkpoints is a cheap accuracy booster justified by flat-minima arguments, adopted for dense tasks with the same recipe as classification.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Weight-space averaging approximates prediction-space averaging only where checkpoint functions are locally affine-compatible; late dense checkpoints agree on interiors (averaging helps via noise reduction) but occupy structurally different boundary hypotheses (averaging weights produces blurred or displaced boundary functions rather than averaged placements), so the benefit decomposes spatially, and the boundary-disagreement amplitude across the averaging window determines whether SWA helps or hurts boundary-sensitive applications.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] On Cityscapes, SWA over the last 20% of training will improve interior accuracy by at least 0.4 while changing 4px-trimap boundary F-score by at most +0.1 or degrading it, at least 70% of SWA's net mIoU gain will come from outside boundary bands, and across configurations varying checkpoint spacing, boundary benefit will correlate negatively (rho <= -0.5) with measured cross-checkpoint boundary disagreement. Kill the idea if boundary metrics improve proportionally with interiors (spatially uniform gains) or the disagreement correlation is absent.
why_important: SWA-style averaging is being adopted wholesale for dense deployment; a spatial decomposition of when averaging helps prevents silent boundary-quality regressions and replaces flat-minima intuition with a checkable adoption criterion for structured outputs.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] SWA's aggregate benefits are established; the spatially-decomposed validity condition and disagreement-based criterion for dense outputs appear new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: SWA at several window/spacing settings on two segmentation setups; decompose gains by region; measure cross-checkpoint prediction disagreement maps; test the correlation between boundary disagreement and boundary benefit.
main_risk: BN statistic recomputation after averaging (standard SWA practice) is itself a boundary-relevant intervention; controlling it separately keeps the weight-averaging effect isolated.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] SWA is a uniformly safe free win, with flat-minima reasoning applied without spatial qualification to structured outputs.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Late checkpoints may be affine-compatible even at boundaries under standard schedules (small final LR), making gains uniform and the caveat empty in practical regimes.
fastest_falsification_experiment: DeepLabv3+ R50 and SegFormer-B0 (public) on Cityscapes (public), 4 SWA settings x 2 architectures x 2 seeds at 40k iterations: about 3 days on one A100; decomposition is post-hoc on saved predictions.
